title: Seeing the same in all (13.19–13.34)
hook: one sun lights the whole world; chapter thirteen says one knower lights every field

segments.voice: Yesterday, amanitva: knowledge starts with humility, first on the Gita's list. Today, the chapter's last and biggest picture.

Noon light falls on a whole street: the parked cars, the dog on the corner, the neighbor nobody gets along with, the trash can, the rose bush. All of it, at once, the same light. The sun doesn't choose. It doesn't get dirty from shining on the trash, or prettier from shining on the roses. Chapter thirteen ends with that picture, its answer to the question it has circled all chapter: who is the knower of the field?
screen: `NOON LIGHT ON A WHOLE STREET.` → `THE ROSE AND THE TRASH CAN.` → `THE SAME LIGHT ON BOTH.`

segments.voice: First, two words the Gita uses a lot from here on. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, the body, the senses, the mind. Purusha: the person, the conscious one who experiences it. Verse twenty: nature is behind all doing; the person is behind the experiencing of pleasure and pain. Then verse twenty-seven, the center of today. The one who sees the supreme Lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, truly sees. Verse twenty-eight follows: samam pashyan, seeing the same Lord everywhere, such a person doesn't harm the self by the self. Commentators unpack that line in more than one way. Some readers hear in it: if the same one lives in everyone, hurting another is hurting yourself. Verse twenty-nine: the one who sees that nature does the acting, and that the self is not the doer, sees. Two pictures close the chapter. Verse thirty-two: space is everywhere, and it's so subtle it's never stained by what it holds. So the self in every body is never stained. Verse thirty-three: as the one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field. One light, many fields. The schools differ again on how literally to take the oneness: Advaita as one self, Vaishnava schools as one Lord dwelling in many selves. Either way, the verse asks for one kind of seeing: look at anyone, and look for the light.
screen: `NATURE ACTS. THE PERSON KNOWS.` · `THE SAME LORD IN ALL BEINGS.` · `HARM NONE, HARM NOT YOURSELF.` · `ONE SUN LIGHTS THE WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `SEEING THE SAME IN ALL.`

segments.voice: Picture a light at your center, steady and warm, then the same light in the person nearest you, in the next room or the next house. Widen it: someone across town, someone on the other side of the world whose name you'll never know, and, if you're willing, someone you find hard. You don't have to like them; just see the same light.
Sama, the same, even. Gita thirteen, twenty-seven: the one who sees the same Lord standing in all beings, imperishable in the perishing, truly sees.
Your line: the one light. It falls on the rose and the trash can alike. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus greet others with namaste, often explained as honoring the divine in the other person; Gita 13.27–13.28, seeing the same Lord in all beings, is one of the verses teachers point to for this.

fork.setup: Krishna wants one picture for how the knower lights every field. what does he choose?
options: the one sun lighting the whole world.
a river flowing into the sea.
fork.reveal: the one sun. verse 33: as one sun lights this whole world, the knower of the field lights the whole field.

original.note: Sanskrit: sama, the same, even; in 13.28, 'samam pashyan', seeing the same everywhere.

trapdoor: what you thought: seeing the same in all means treating everyone identically.
what it means: seeing one light, the same Lord, in every being, and so not harming the self by the self.
what a scholar hears: 13.27–13.28 use 'samam' twice; 13.32–13.33 give the images of space (akasha) and the one sun; Advaita and Vishishtadvaita read the oneness differently.
guess: the same, even: seeing one Lord alike in all beings
treating every person in exactly the same way
calm, an inner peace that nothing can disturb
recall: time, which brings all things to an end
